name: TPE system

title: Remark
body_md:
The primary structural advantage of the TPE system lies in the form of its most complicated equation~\eqref{eq:two_beta_identity}: it equates a sum of quadratic terms to a single cubic term, whereas the corresponding equation in Izumi's system equates a sum of cubic terms to a single quadratic term. While such a shift might appear minor in a general polynomial system, it is crucial in the near-group setting, where this is the \emph{sole} non-trivial equation governing the system.

    This structural simplification provides substantial theoretical and computational leverage. For instance, in characteristic two, setting $g=2h$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:two_beta_identity} directly yields the Frobenius relation $\beta(2h)=\beta(h)^4$. Crucially, the fundamental role of the TPE framework is further validated by the work of Radchenko and Wheeler \cite{RadchenkoWheeler}, who constructed solutions to Izumi's subsystem by first establishing that they satisfy an equation analogous to TPE-equation~\eqref{eq:two_beta_identity}, rather than tackling the pentagon equations directly.

title: Theorem
body_md: Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of order $n$. The existence of a spherical (resp., unitary) near-group fusion category with fusion rules $G + n$ and trivial Frobenius--Schur indicator over a field $K$ (resp., $\mathbb{C}$) is equivalent to the solvability of the TPE system (resp., the unitary TPE system).

title: Remark
body_md: The primary constraint \eqref{eq:two_beta_identity} in the TPE system equates a sum of products of two terms of $ \beta $ to a product of three terms of $ \beta $. Remarkably, the Belousov--Sarkissian--Spiridonov (BSS) identity exhibits the exact same algebraic structure, expressing an integral of a product of two terms of $ \gamma $ as a product of three terms of $ \gamma $. This striking structural parallel provides the key motivation for constructing $\beta$ via hyperbolic gamma functions $ \gamma(z) $.

label: prop:cubic-reduction
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:cubic-reduction}\label{prop:beta-normalization}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of order $n$, over a field $K$ in
which $n$ is invertible. Fix a nondegenerate symmetric bicharacter
$\chi$, an even quadratic refinement $a$ satisfying
\eqref{eq:apm}--\eqref{eq:achi}, and $d\ne0$ with $d^2=n+nd$; put $d_\varrho=d$.
Then the TPE system is equivalent to
\[
 \beta(0)=-d^{-1}
\]
and the cubic equation~\eqref{eq:two_beta_identity}. More precisely,
these conditions force $B:=\sum_{g\in G}\beta(g)\ne0$, and the
remaining equations hold with the unique choice
\[
 c=-\frac1{dB}.
\]
Every $\beta(g)$ is then nonzero, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:beta-zero-convolution}
 \beta(0)=-\frac1d,\qquad
 \sum_{k\in G}\frac{\beta(g-k)\beta(k)}{a(k)}
 =\delta_{g,0}-\frac1d.
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: A single cubic identity

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $b=\beta(0)=-1/d$ and
$q(g)=\beta(g)\beta(-g)/a(g)$. Thus $q(-g)=q(g)$. For the
unnormalized Fourier transform
\[
 (\mathcal Ff)(h)=\sum_{k\in G}\chi(h,k)^{-1}f(k),
\]
character orthogonality gives $\mathcal F^2q=nq$,
$\mathcal F\delta_0=\mathbf1$, and $\mathcal F\mathbf1=n\delta_0$.
The case $g=0$ of the cubic identity, divided by $a(h)/n$, is
\[
 \mathcal Fq=nbq+\frac nd\delta_0.
\]
Applying $\mathcal F$ again gives
\[
 (1-nb^2)q=\frac{nb}{d}\delta_0+\frac1d\mathbf1.
\]
Since $1-nb^2=n/d$, this is precisely
\[
 q=\frac1n\mathbf1-\frac1d\delta_0,
\]
which proves~\eqref{eq:betapm} and nonvanishing of every $\beta(g)$.

Put
\[
 C_h=\sum_{g\in G}\frac{\beta(g)\beta(h-g)}{a(h-g)}.
\]
The case $h=0$ of the cubic equation, with its other argument renamed,
now gives
\[
 C_h=nbq(h)+\frac nd\delta_{h,0}=b+\delta_{h,0},
\]
using $n/d+n/d^2=1$. Divide the cubic equation by $a(h-g)$ and sum
over $g$ to obtain
\[
 \frac Bn\sum_{k\in G}\chi(h,k)^{-1}\frac{\beta(k)}{a(k)}
 =\beta(-h)C_h+\frac{\delta_{h,0}}d=b\beta(-h).
\]
At $h=0$ the right side is $b^2\ne0$, so $B\ne0$.
Replacing $h$ by $-h$ proves~\eqref{eq:Fourier} for $c=b/B$.

Finally, set $S_a=\sum_g a(g)$, $S_{a^{-1}}=\sum_g a(g)^{-1}$,
and
\[
 (Tf)(h)=\sum_g a(g)^{-1}\chi(h,g)f(g).
\]
The refinement identity and character orthogonality give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scalar-fourier-toolkit}
 S_aS_{a^{-1}}=n,\qquad
 (T^2)_{h,j}=S_{a^{-1}}a(h)\chi(h,j)^{-1},\qquad
 T^3=nS_{a^{-1}}I.
\end{equation}
Since $T\beta=cn\beta$ and $\beta\ne0$, we get
$c^3S_a=1/n$, proving~\eqref{eq:c_nonzero}.

Conversely, suppose the full scalar system holds. Its quadratic
identity gives $\beta(0)^2=1/n-1/d=1/d^2$. At $(g,h)=(0,0)$
the cubic identity then gives $\beta(0)^3=-1/d^3$, whence
$\beta(0)=-1/d$. The displayed summed cubic identity and the
Fourier equation force $c=b/B$, proving uniqueness.

label: prop:F-identities
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:F-identities}\label{prop:sF-well-defined}
The function $F$ satisfies
\[
 F(z)=\gamma(\omega_1-z),\qquad F(z)F(n-z)=1,\qquad
 F(z+n)=\frac{\sin(\pi z/\omega_1)}{\sin(\pi z/\omega_2)}F(z).
\]
For every nonzero integer $m$,
\[
 F(m+n)=(-1)^mF(m),\qquad F(-m)=\frac{(-1)^m}{F(m)}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
 F(0)=\frac{\sqrt n}{\omega_2},\qquad
 F(0)^2-1=\sqrt n\,F(0),\qquad F(k)>0\quad(0\leq k<n).
\]
The product $s(x)F(x)$ is $n$-periodic on
$\mathbb Z\setminus n\mathbb Z$. The zero residue class is exceptional:
$F(n)=F(0)^{-1}\ne F(0)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Reflection gives the first two identities, and the two gamma shifts give
\[
 \frac{F(z+n)}{F(z)}
 =\frac{\gamma(\omega_2+z)}{\gamma(\omega_1+z)}
 =\frac{\sin(\pi z/\omega_1)}{\sin(\pi z/\omega_2)}.
\]
At a nonzero integer $m$, the sines do not vanish and their ratio is
$(-1)^m$, since $1/\omega_2-1/\omega_1=1$.
Reflection then gives the formula for $F(-m)$, while
$s(m+n)=(-1)^m s(m)$ proves periodicity on the nonzero classes.
Taking $z\to0$ in~\eqref{eq:gamma-shift1} and using the residue at zero
gives $F(0)=\gamma(\omega_1)=\sqrt n/\omega_2$.
The equation $\omega_2^2+n\omega_2=n$ proves its quadratic identity,
and~\eqref{eq:gamma-positivity} proves positivity.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 1: the finite sum as a residue sum.}

Put
\[
A:=\frac{\pi(g-2h)}{n},
\]
and choose \(\phi\in(-\pi,\pi]\) such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:phi-direct}
\phi\equiv\pi-A\pmod{2\pi}.
\end{equation}
Then
\[
(-1)^k e^{-i\phi k}=e^{iAk},
\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.
\]

Define
\[
R_g(z):=\frac{F(z)}{F(z-g)},
\qquad
K_g(z):=
\frac{\pi e^{-i\phi z}}{\sin\pi z}R_g(z),
\qquad
J_g(z):=
e^{-i\phi z}\gamma(-z)\gamma(z-g).
\]

Let
\[
L:=\left\lfloor\frac{g}{\omega_2}\right\rfloor
\]
and choose
\[
0<\varepsilon<
\min\{1,(L+1)\omega_2-g\},
\qquad
\sigma:=-\varepsilon.
\]
In the strip
\[
\sigma<\mathrm{Re} (z)<\sigma+n,
\]
the poles of \(K_g\) are
\[
0,1,\ldots,n-1
\]
and
\[
p_\ell:=g-\ell\omega_2,
\qquad
1\leq\ell\leq L.
\]
The points \(p_\ell\) are nonintegral by the irrationality of \(\omega_2\).

At an integer \(k\),
\[
\operatorname{Res}_{z=k}K_g(z)
=
e^{iAk}R_g(k).
\]
For \(k\neq g\),
\[
R_g(k)
=
(-1)^{g-k}F(k)F(g-k),
\]
whereas
\[
R_g(g)=\frac{F(g)}{F(0)}.
\]
Therefore
\begin{align}
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\operatorname{Res}_{z=k}K_g(z)
&=
(-1)^gS_{g,h}
+
(1-F(0)^2)e^{iAg}\frac{F(g)}{F(0)}.
\label{eq:integer-residues-direct}
\end{align}

The vertical asymptotics of the hyperbolic gamma function give, uniformly on the strip,
\[
R_g(x+iy)
=
O\left(e^{-\pi g|y|/n}\right),
\]
and hence
\[
K_g(x+iy)
=
O\left(
e^{-[\pi(1+g/n)-|\phi|]|y|}
\right).
\]
Thus the horizontal sides of the residue rectangle vanish as its height tends to infinity.

Using
\[
R_g(z)
=
-4
\sin\frac{\pi z}{\omega_2}
\sin\frac{\pi(z-g)}{\omega_1}
\gamma(-z)\gamma(z-g),
\]
together with
\[
\frac1{\omega_2}-\frac1{\omega_1}=1,
\]
one obtains
\[
K_g(z+n)-K_g(z)
=
-4\pi
\sin\frac{\pi g}{\omega_1}
J_g(z).
\]
Consequently, the residue theorem on the rectangle $\mathcal R_R$ (shown in Figure~\ref{fig:residue-strip}) gives
\begin{align}
&\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\operatorname{Res}_{z=k}K_g(z)
+
\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}
\operatorname{Res}_{z=p_\ell}K_g(z)
=
-2\sin\frac{\pi g}{\omega_1}
\int_{\sigma-i\infty}^{\sigma+i\infty}
J_g(z)\frac{dz}{i}.
\label{eq:rectangle-direct}
\end{align}

Write
\[
r_\ell
:=
\operatorname{Res}_{z=p_\ell}J_g(z),
\qquad
0\leq\ell\leq L,
\]
where \(p_0=g\). A direct substitution of
\(p_\ell=g-\ell\omega_2\) gives
\[
\operatorname{Res}_{z=p_\ell}K_g(z)
=
4\pi
\sin\frac{\pi g}{\omega_1}\,r_\ell,
\qquad
1\leq\ell\leq L.
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sigma-direct}
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\operatorname{Res}_{z=k}K_g(z)
=
-2\sin\frac{\pi g}{\omega_1}I_\sigma
-
4\pi\sin\frac{\pi g}{\omega_1}
\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}r_\ell,
\end{equation}
where
\[
I_\sigma
:=
\int_{\sigma-i\infty}^{\sigma+i\infty}
J_g(z)\frac{dz}{i}.
\]

Now deform the contour $ \mathrm{Re} (z) = \sigma $ to a separating contour \(C_{\rm sep}(g)\) (shown in Figure~\ref{fig:separating-contour}) for the two pole families of $ J_g(z) $
\[
g-j\omega_1-k\omega_2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
j\omega_1+k\omega_2.
\]
The deformation crosses precisely
\[
p_0,p_1,\ldots,p_L,
\]
and therefore
\[
I_{\rm sep}
=
I_\sigma
+
2\pi\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}r_\ell.
\]
Substituting this into \eqref{eq:sigma-direct}, all nonintegral residues cancel, and we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:direct-Isep}
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\operatorname{Res}_{z=k}K_g(z)
=
-2\sin\frac{\pi g}{\omega_1}\,I_{\rm sep}
+
4\pi\sin\frac{\pi g}{\omega_1}\,r_0.
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 2: meromorphic continuation of the separating-contour integral.}

For independent complex parameters \(g,\alpha\), consider
\begin{equation}\label{eq:BSS-family}
\mathcal I(g,\alpha)
:=
\int_{C_{\rm sep}(g)}
e^{\pi i z(2\alpha-g-\Omega)/n}
\gamma(z-g)\gamma(-z)\frac{dz}{i\sqrt n}.
\end{equation}
The contour $C_{\rm sep}(g)$ is precisely the separating contour used
in $I_{\rm sep}$.
For \(\mathrm{Re} (g)<0\), the two pole families
\[
g-j\omega_1-k\omega_2
\]
and
\[
j\omega_1+k\omega_2
\]
are separated by a vertical contour $ \mathrm{Re} (z) = \sigma $. The integral is therefore well defined in a nonempty open region of the \((g,\alpha)\)-plane where the convergence conditions of the BSS formula are satisfied.

On compact subsets avoiding pole collisions, the separating contour may be chosen continuously in the parameters, and the vertical asymptotics of the hyperbolic gamma function imply locally uniform convergence. Hence \(\mathcal I(g,\alpha)\) is holomorphic there. Continuing the contour across a pole changes the integral by the corresponding residue; consequently \(\mathcal I(g,\alpha)\) admits a meromorphic continuation in the parameters.

A collision between the two pole families can occur only when
\[
g\in\omega_1\mathbb Z+\omega_2\mathbb Z.
\]
By
\[
(\omega_1\mathbb Z+\omega_2\mathbb Z)\cap\mathbb Z=n\mathbb Z,
\]
none of \(1,\ldots,n-1\) is a collision point. Thus the separating-contour integral may be continued from \(\mathrm{Re} (g)<0\) to each
\[
g=1,\ldots,n-1.
\]

The BSS identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:BSS_identity}) gives
\begin{align}
\mathcal I(g,\alpha)
&=
e^{\pi i g(2\alpha-g-\Omega)/(2n)}
\gamma(\alpha)
\gamma(\Omega+g-\alpha)
\gamma(-g).
\label{eq:BSS-meromorphic}
\end{align}
Both sides are meromorphic in \(g\) and \(\alpha\), so the identity remains valid under the above continuation.

For our fixed integers \(g,h\), choose
\[
\alpha
=
\frac{\Omega+g}{2}
-\frac{n\phi}{2\pi}.
\]
Then
\[
\frac{\pi i}{n}(2\alpha-g-\Omega)z
=
-i\phi z,
\]
and hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Isep-direct}
I_{\rm sep}
=
\sqrt n\,
e^{-ig\phi/2}
\gamma(-g)
\gamma(\alpha)
\gamma(\Omega+g-\alpha).
\end{equation}

Moreover,
\[
r_0
=
\frac{\sqrt n}{2\pi}
e^{-i\phi g}\gamma(-g).
\]
Using
\[
2\sin\frac{\pi g}{\omega_1}\gamma(-g)
=
(-1)^{g+1}F(g),
\]
equation \eqref{eq:direct-Isep} becomes
\begin{align}
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\operatorname{Res}_{z=k}K_g(z)
&=
(-1)^g\sqrt n\,
e^{-ig\phi/2}
F(g)
\gamma(\alpha)
\gamma(\Omega+g-\alpha)
+
(-1)^{g+1}\sqrt n\,
e^{-i\phi g}F(g).
\label{eq:residues-BSS-direct}
\end{align}
Since
\[
e^{-i\phi g}
=
(-1)^ge^{iAg}
\]
and
\[
\frac{1-F(0)^2}{F(0)}
=
-\sqrt n,
\]
the second term in \eqref{eq:residues-BSS-direct} is exactly the correction term in \eqref{eq:integer-residues-direct}. Cancelling these correction terms gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S-BSS-direct}
S_{g,h}
=
\sqrt n\,
e^{-ig\phi/2}
F(g)
\gamma(\alpha)
\gamma(\Omega+g-\alpha).
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Step 3: the special choice of \(\alpha\).}

Set
\[
\eta
=
\begin{cases}
0,&2h\leq g,\\
1,&2h>g.
\end{cases}
\]
Since
\[
\phi
\equiv
\pi-\frac{\pi(g-2h)}n
\pmod{2\pi},
\]
we have
\[
\phi
=
\pi-\frac{\pi(g-2h)}n-2\pi\eta.
\]
Using
\[
\Omega-n=2\omega_2,
\qquad
\Omega+n=2\omega_1,
\]
we obtain
\begin{align}
\alpha
&=
\omega_2+g-h+n\eta,
\label{eq:alpha-special}\\
\Omega+g-\alpha
&=
\omega_1+h-n\eta.
\label{eq:beta-special}
\end{align}
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gamma-product-direct}
\gamma(\alpha)\gamma(\Omega+g-\alpha)
=
\frac{F(-h+n\eta)}
     {F(g-h+n\eta)}.
\end{equation}

The integer identities
\[
F(x)F(n-x)=1,
\qquad
F(x+n)=(-1)^xF(x)\quad(x\neq0),
\]
together with
\[
s(x+n)=(-1)^x s(x),
\]
give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:phase-conversion-direct}
e^{-ig\phi/2}
\frac{F(-h+n\eta)}
     {F(g-h+n\eta)}
=
\frac{s(\overline{-h})}
     {s(\overline{g-h})}
F(\overline{-h})F(\overline{h-g}).
\end{equation}
The boundary case \(g-h=0\) is interpreted using
\[
F(n)=F(0)^{-1}.
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:phase-conversion-direct} holds for all
\(0\leq h<n\).

Substituting \eqref{eq:phase-conversion-direct} into
\eqref{eq:S-BSS-direct} proves
\[
S_{g,h}
=
\sqrt n\,F(g)
\frac{s(\overline{-h})}
     {s(\overline{g-h})}
F(\overline{-h})F(\overline{h-g}),
\]
as required.

\label{prop:abelian-refinements}
Let $G=\bigoplus_{i=1}^r\mathbb Z/m_i\mathbb Z\,e_i$ and let
$\chi:G\times G\to\mathbb T$ be a symmetric bicharacter. Choose
$\xi_i$ with
\[
 \xi_i^2=\chi(e_i,e_i),\qquad \xi_i^{m_i^2}=1.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abelian-quadratic-formula}
 a\!\left(\sum_i x_ie_i\right)
 =\prod_i\xi_i^{-x_i^2}
  \prod_{i<j}\chi(e_i,e_j)^{-x_ix_j}
\end{equation}
is a well-defined even quadratic refinement of $\chi$. Such refinements
form a torsor for $\operatorname{Hom}(G,\{\pm1\})$; in particular
there are exactly $|G[2]|$ of them. If $|G|$ is odd, the unique one is
$a(g)=\chi(g/2,g)^{-1}$.
head: environment
name: All even quadratic refinements

title: Proof
body_md:
If $m_i$ is odd, there is a unique permissible square root,
$\xi_i=\chi(e_i,e_i)^{(m_i+1)/2}$. If $m_i$ is even, both square
roots satisfy the required power condition. Increasing $x_i$ by $m_i$
does not change the diagonal factor because
$\xi_i^{2m_ix_i+m_i^2}=1$, or a mixed factor because
$\chi(e_i,e_j)^{m_i}=1$. Thus the formula is well defined. Negation
preserves it, and expansion of $(x_i+y_i)^2$ gives
$a(x+y)\chi(x,y)=a(x)a(y)$, including the mixed terms.
The quotient of two refinements is a character. Evenness says that
this character has square $1$, and conversely multiplying by any
such character preserves all requirements. Finally,
$|\operatorname{Hom}(G,\{\pm1\})|=|G/2G|=|G[2]|$.
For odd-order $G$, division by $2$ is unique; the stated formula has
the required polarization, and uniqueness follows from $G[2]=0$.

label: lem:algebraic-reflection
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Algebraic reflection on scalar solutions

title: Proof
body_md:
The dimension and quadratic-refinement data are preserved by substitution,
as is $\beta(0)=-1/d$. If $E(g,h)$ denotes the left side minus the
right side of~\eqref{eq:two_beta_identity}, substitution and the change
$k\mapsto-k$ give
\[
 E_\tau(g,h)=\frac{E(-g,h-g)}{a(g)a(h)a(h-g)}.
\]
The denominator equals $1$ on the support of the exceptional term.
Proposition~\ref{prop:cubic-reduction} therefore supplies all the remaining
equations. To identify the new value of $c$, use the original Fourier
equation at zero and evenness of $a$:
\[
 \sum_g\beta_\tau(g)=\sum_g\frac{\beta(g)}{a(g)}=cn\beta(0),
 \qquad
 c_\tau=\frac{\beta_\tau(0)}{\sum_g\beta_\tau(g)}=\frac1{nc}.
\]
Applying $\tau$ twice fixes every parameter.

label: lem:izumi-cubic-dictionary
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Fourier form of the cubic identity

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $E(g,h)$ be the residual of~\eqref{eq:two_beta_identity} and let
$D(u,v)$ be the residual of~\eqref{eq:izumi-cubic-form}, in each case
left side minus right side. Expanding $\beta(t+v)$ by the Fourier
equation and applying the product relation gives
\[
 D(u,v)=\frac1c\sum_{s\in G}\chi(v,s)
       \frac{\beta(s)}{a(s)a(s-u)}E(u,s).
\]
Every $\beta(s)$ is nonzero by the product relation and
$\beta(0)=-1/d$. Character orthogonality gives the inverse
\[
 E(u,s)=\frac{c\,a(s)a(s-u)}{n\beta(s)}
         \sum_{v\in G}\chi(v,s)^{-1}D(u,v).
\]
Thus the two residual systems vanish simultaneously over $K$.

label: lem:mixed-gauge
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:mixed-gauge}
There are unitary morphisms
\[
 m_{g,h}:g\otimes h\longrightarrow g+h,\qquad
 L_g:g\otimes\varrho\longrightarrow\varrho,\qquad
 R_g:\varrho\otimes g\longrightarrow\varrho
\]
for which the associativity coefficients on $(g,h,k)$, $(g,h,\varrho)$,
and $(\varrho,g,h)$ are $1$.
head: environment
name: Coherent mixed vertices

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose the $L_g$ unitarily, with $L_0$ the unit constraint. Define
$m_{g,h}$ by requiring the two composites
$(g\otimes h)\otimes\varrho\to\varrho$ to agree after inserting the
associator. This determines a unitary $m_{g,h}$, since the relevant
morphism spaces are one-dimensional. The pentagon on $(g,h,k,\varrho)$
then makes the $m_{g,h}$ associative. Thus the pointed associator and
the left module associator are simultaneously trivialized.

The right maps must also respect the bends. Let
$t:\mathbf1\to\varrho\otimes\varrho$ be the standard coevaluation, so
$t^\dagger t=d$. Define $U_g:\varrho\to\varrho\otimes g$ by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mixed-mate-normalization}
 (\operatorname{id}_\varrho\otimes L_g)
 (U_g\otimes\operatorname{id}_\varrho)t=t,
 \qquad R_g=U_g^\dagger.
\end{equation}
Rigidity makes the displayed assignment from $U_g$ to its left-hand
side an isomorphism of one-dimensional morphism spaces, so $U_g$
exists uniquely. If $U_g^\dagger U_g=s\operatorname{id}_\varrho$,
taking the squared norm in this equation gives $sd=d$; hence $U_g$
is unitary. Apply the same defining equation successively to $U_h$
and $U_g$, and use the left module relation. Uniqueness gives
\[
 (\operatorname{id}_\varrho\otimes m_{g,h})
 (U_g\otimes\operatorname{id}_h)U_h=U_{g+h}.
\]
Taking adjoints proves the right module relation. This is the
categorical normalization of \cite[Remark~3.2]{Izumi2017}; it fixes
both module associativity and the mixed bends, rather than choosing
their phases independently. Associators have been suppressed in
these formulas by coherence.

Choose its fusion map to the simple object $a\otimes g$ unitarily and

which gives \eqref{eq:mixed-splitting} (the label $ag$ denotes

label: cor: rhorhorho
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Normal form

title: Proof
body_md:
The commuting unitary operators $\pi_z(g)$ have simultaneous weight
spaces indexed by $\widehat G$. The relation
$\pi_z(g)\pi_x(h)=\chi(g,h)\pi_x(h)\pi_z(g)$ permutes these
spaces by multiplication by $\chi(-,h)$. Nondegeneracy of $\chi$
therefore implies that all $n$ weights occur, with the same
multiplicity. Since $\dim V=n$, each weight space is one-dimensional.
Choose a unit vector $v_0$ of trivial weight and put
$v_h=\pi_x(h)v_0$. The first two displayed formulas follow, and the
basis is orthonormal.

Applying $ Eq.~\eqref{equ:yz} $ to $ v_k $. We obtain
\begin{align*}
  \pi_z(h)\pi_y(g)v_k = \chi(h,k-g)\pi_y(g)v_k.
\end{align*}
Thus \(\pi_y(g)v_k\) is a simultaneous eigenvector of $ \pi_z(h) $ with eigenvalue $ \chi(h,k-g) $. Hence,
\begin{align*}
  \pi_y(g)v_k = c(g,k)v_{k-g},
\end{align*}
for some scalar \(c(g,k)\).
Next, applying $ Eq.~\eqref{equ: xy} $ to $ v_k $. We get
\begin{align*}
  c(h,k) = \chi(g,h)c(h,g+k).
\end{align*} 
Multiplying by $ \chi(h,k) $ on both sides, we obtain
\begin{align*}
  \chi(h,k)c(h,k) = \chi(h,g+k)c(h,g+k).
\end{align*}
Thus the quantity \(\chi(h,k)c(h,k)\) is independent of \(k\). Denote its common value by \(t(h)\).
Then we obtain
\[
 \pi_y(g)v_h=t(g)\chi(g,h)^{-1}v_{h-g}.
\]
The representation law for $\pi_y$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abelian-t-cocycle}
 t(g+h)=t(g)t(h)\chi(g,h).
\end{equation}
Thus $a=t^{-1}$ satisfies the quadratic relation, but evenness still
requires the theta pairing.

For every $l\in G$, the group-loop insertion gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:theta-selection-chain}
 \ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D042\endcsname}}}=\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D043\endcsname}}}=\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D044\endcsname}}}
 =\chi(l,h+k)\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D042\endcsname}}}.
\end{equation}
By nondegeneracy,
$B(v_h,v_k)=0$ unless $h+k=0$, or pictorially
\begin{equation}\label{equ: delta hk}
 \ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D045\endcsname}}}=0\qquad(h+k\ne0).
\end{equation}
Write
$b_h=B(v_h,v_{-h})\ne0$. The mixed fusion--splitting cancellation is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:theta-slide-right}
 \ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D046\endcsname}}}=\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D047\endcsname}}}
 =t(g)\chi(g,h)^{-1}\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D048\endcsname}}}.
\end{equation}
Consequently
\[
 b_h=t(g)\chi(g,h)^{-1}b_{h-g}.
\]
The theta pairing is symmetric by the pivotal-pairing formula of \cite[\S3.3]{LPR} and $\nu_2(\varrho)=1$, so $b_g=b_{-g}$. Taking $h=0$ and $h=g$ gives
\[
 b_0=t(g)b_{-g},\qquad b_g=t(g)\chi(g,g)^{-1}b_0.
\]
Hence $t(g)^2=\chi(g,g)$ and $b_g/b_0=t(g)^{-1}=a(g)$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:abelian-t-cocycle} at $(g,-g)$ now gives
$t(-g)=t(g)$, proving evenness. Finally,
$a(h)/a(h-g)=a(g)^{-1}\chi(g,h)^{-1}$, which proves the third
normal-form identity.

label: eq:rho-rho-matrix-units
title: Proof
body_md:
Resolving the central channel gives the following basis of
$\operatorname{Hom}(\varrho\otimes\varrho,\varrho\otimes\varrho)$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rho-rho-matrix-units}
 E_{h,k}:=\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D069\endcsname}}}\quad(h,k\in G),
 \qquad P_l:=\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D070\endcsname}}}\quad(l\in G).
\end{equation}
Here $E_{h,k}$ has lower label $k$ and upper label $h'$.
Write the horizontal diagram as $H_g:=\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D066\endcsname}}}$.  Its expansion
is
\begin{equation}\label{equ: coef}
 H_g=\sum_{h,k\in G}C^g_{h,k}E_{h,k}
       +\sum_{l\in G}f_l^gP_l.
\end{equation}
The trace normalization of the vertices gives
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(E_{h,k}E_{p,q})
    =d_\varrho^{-1}\delta_{k,p}\delta_{h,q}.
\]
Thus the coefficient $C^g_{h,k}$ is obtained by pairing with
$E_{k,h}=\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D071\endcsname}}}$, and its closure is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:extract-rho-coefficient}
 \ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D072\endcsname}}}
 =\operatorname{tr}(E_{k,h}H_g)=\frac{C^g_{h,k}}{d_\varrho}.
\end{equation}
The primed label is the trace-dual vertex; using
$v_{-k}=a(k)v_k'$ with its prescribed bends, the triangular face of
this closure has total charge $h-k$.  Lemma~\ref{lem: ghk} therefore
gives $C^g_{h,k}=0$ whenever $h\ne k$.

For the invertible channels, close
$\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D073\endcsname}}}$ against $\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D074\endcsname}}}$.
The mixed tetrahedral evaluation and the same trace normalization give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:extract-invertible-coefficient}
 d_\varrho^2 f_l^g=\chi(-l,0)\delta_{g,0}=\delta_{g,0}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, with $C_h^g=C^g_{h,h}$,
\begin{equation}\label{equ: coef1}
 \ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D066\endcsname}}}
 =\sum_{h\in G}C_h^g\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D067\endcsname}}}
   +\frac{\delta_{g,0}}{d_\varrho^2}\sum_{l\in G}\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D070\endcsname}}}.
\end{equation}

It remains to compare the diagonal coefficients.  We extract the
zero-diagonal term from the strand-decorated diagram:
\[
 \ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D075\endcsname}}}\quad\text{in}\quad\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D076\endcsname}}}.
\]
Sliding the invertible strand first gives, by
Corollary~\ref{cor: rhorhorho},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:beta-character-slide}
 \ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D076\endcsname}}}=\chi(h,g)^{-1}\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D066\endcsname}}},
\end{equation}
so that coefficient is $\chi(h,g)^{-1}C_0^g$.
Alternatively, expand the horizontal diagram first.  Only its
$h$-diagonal term contributes, because the strand translates both
indices by $-h$.  Its reduction is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:beta-diagonal-slide}
 \ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D077\endcsname}}}=\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D078\endcsname}}}=\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D075\endcsname}}}.
\end{equation}
Here the two dual vertex factors cancel by
Proposition~\ref{pro: normalization}; the normalization at $0$ is
$v_0'=v_0$, after the specified bending identification.
The coefficient is therefore $C_h^g$.
It follows that $C_h^g=\chi(h,g)^{-1}C_0^g$.  Defining
$\beta(g)=C_0^g$ proves \eqref{equ: real parameter}.

body_md:
The first two rows are Lemmas~\ref{lem: F-symbol 6 inv}
and~\ref{lem: bicha}.  The one-invertible-edge row follows by sliding
its strand and pairing the remaining dual basis vertices.  After this
slide, the two lower corners in the middle picture are bivalent bends;
the picture is a closed theta graph:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:one-edge-table-proof}
 \ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D079\endcsname}}}
 =\chi(g,h)\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D081\endcsname}}}
 =\chi(g,h)\delta_{h,k}.
\end{equation}
For the last row, closing the expansion in
Lemma~\ref{pro: real parameter} gives the value with one zero vertex:
\begin{equation}\label{equ: 6rho fsymbol easy}
 \ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D082\endcsname}}}=\chi(h,k)^{-1}\frac{\beta(k)}{d_\varrho}.
\end{equation}
Retain the abbreviations $p=h-g$ and $r=k-g$. Insert the three
$g$-labelled strands and slide them to the adjacent vertices.  The normalized group action produces the two ratios of
quadratic factors:
\begin{align}
 \ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D080\endcsname}}}&=\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D083\endcsname}}},\notag\\
 &=\frac{a(h-g)}{a(h)}\frac{a(k-g)}{a(k)}\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D082\endcsname}}},\notag\\
 &=\frac{a(h-g)a(k-g)}{a(h)a(k)}\,
    \chi(h,k)^{-1}\frac{\beta(k)}{d_\varrho}.
    \label{eq:no-edge-table-proof}
\end{align}
It remains to check that these representatives cover all admissible
edge types.  At a trivalent vertex, exactly two invertible incident
edges would force the third edge to be invertible.  Thus the
invertible-edge subgraph of a tetrahedron can only consist of all six
edges, a three-edge star, two disjoint edges, one edge, or no edge.
The orientation-preserving tetrahedral symmetry group is transitive
on the configurations of each type.  Its action, with the indicated
corner and duality transports, reduces the first four types to
\eqref{eq:table-three-invertibles}--\eqref{eq:table-one-invertible}.

For the last type, choose the corners used in
\eqref{eq:table-no-invertible}, and write its labels as $u,v,w',z$
at the lower left, lower right, top, and interior vertices,
respectively.  The left triangular face has charge $u+z-w$, since
the primed vertex is $a(w)^{-1}v_{-w}$ after bending.  Its value is
therefore zero unless $w=u+z$.  In the remaining case, put
$g=u$, $h=w$ and $k=u+v$.  The four labels are precisely
$g,r,h',p$, with $r=k-g$ and $p=h-g$, as in \eqref{eq:table-no-invertible}.
This proves completeness in the fixed corner convention; arbitrary
corners are obtained by \eqref{eq:vertex-rotation} and the duality maps.

label: eq:beta-zero-face
title: Proof
body_md:
Specialize \eqref{equ: 6rho fsymbol easy} at $h=0$ and $k=g$.
It defines a coefficient functional $\ell$ on the trivalent space:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:beta-zero-face}
 \ell(v_g):=
 d_\varrho\left.\ensuremath{\vcenter{\hbox{\csname ngdiagram@D082\endcsname}}}\right|_{h=0,\,k=g}
 =\beta(g).
\end{equation}
The three vertices of the face opposite the $g$-vertex have label $0$,
with the prime at the top interpreted using $v_0'=v_0$.  Their marked
corners all point into this same triangular face.

Rotate the tetrahedron by the order-three symmetry which fixes the
$g$-vertex and cyclically permutes the opposite face.  The three
zero-labelled vertices, with their inward-facing corners, are
permuted without a coefficient.  At the fixed vertex this symmetry
induces a cyclic change of its marked corner.  It follows that
$\ell\circ R=\ell$ (the opposite choice of cyclic direction gives the
equivalent identity with $R^{-1}$).  Expanding that corner change by
\eqref{eq:vertex-rotation} gives
\[
 \beta(g)=\ell(Rv_g)
 =c a(g)\sum_{h\in G}\chi(g,h)^{-1}\ell(v_h),
\]
which is \eqref{eq:beta-rotation}.

Finally, take the adjoint of the closed diagram in
\eqref{eq:beta-zero-face}, and use the reflection which interchanges
the two zero-labelled vertices in the marked face at the $g$-vertex.
This reflection fixes that vertex and its marked face, so no further
corner rotation occurs there.  Reflection changes each vertex to its
trace-dual vertex.  The three zero-labelled vertices remain unchanged;
the fourth becomes $v_g'$.  The trace-orthonormal normalization and
$v_g'=a(g)^{-1}v_{-g}$ therefore give
\[
 \overline{\beta(g)}=\ell(v_g')
 =a(g)^{-1}\ell(v_{-g})=a(g)^{-1}\beta(-g).
\]

name: Transport of the marked tetrahedra

label: eq:algebraic-tetra-tensor
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $A,B,C,D$ for the lower-left, lower-right, top and interior
vertices, respectively. The all-$\varrho$ coefficient, with labels
$v_u,v_v,v_w',v_z$ at these vertices, is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:algebraic-tetra-tensor}
 T(u,v;w,z)=\delta_{w,u+z}
 \frac{a(z)a(v)}{a(w)a(u+v)}
 \chi(w,u+v)^{-1}\frac{\beta(u+v)}d.
\end{equation}
To check proper transport, use unprimed labels at all four vertices:
\[
 W(u,v,w,z)=a(w)T(u,v;-w,z)
 =\delta_{u+w+z,0}\frac{a(z)a(v)}{d\,a(u+v)}
       \chi(w,u+v)\beta(u+v).
\]
The marked faces are $ACD$ at $A,C,D$ and $BCD$ at $B$.
The generators $(A\,C\,D)$ and $(A\,B)(C\,D)$ of $A_4$ therefore
require, respectively,
\begin{align}
 W(u,v,w,z)&=\sum_j(R^2)_{jv}W(z,j,u,w),
       \label{eq:proper-tetra-three-cycle}\\
 W(u,v,w,z)&=\sum_{j,k}(R^2)_{jz}R_{kw}W(v,u,j,k).
       \label{eq:proper-tetra-double-transposition}
\end{align}
Indeed, $R^2_{jv}=\chi(j,v)/(nc\,a(j))$ reduces the first sum to
\[
 \delta_{u+w+z,0}\frac{a(w)\chi(-z,v)}{nc d}
 \sum_t\chi(u+v,t)\frac{\beta(t)}{a(t)}
 =\delta_{u+w+z,0}\frac{a(w)\chi(-z,v)}d\beta(u+v).
\]
The Fourier equation gives the equality, and the quadratic relation
identifies this with $W$. In the second sum, set $m=u+v$ and first
use the charge constraint. The remaining sum is
\[
 \frac{a(w)a(u)\beta(m)}{nd\,a(m)}
 \sum_j\frac{a(v+j)}{a(j)}
       \chi(j,z)\chi(w,v+j)\chi(j,m).
\]
Its inner sum is
$n a(v)\chi(w,v)\delta_{u+w+z,0}$ by character orthogonality;
the quadratic relation again gives $W$.

For the mixed rows it suffices to check their proper support
stabilizers. With
$U(g;h,k)=\chi(g,h)\delta_{h,k}$ and $V(g,h)=d\chi(g,h)$,
the only nontrivial stabilizer of the single-edge support is
$(A\,B)(C\,D)$. Its coefficient identity is
\[
 \frac{a(h)}{a(k)}U(-g;-k,-h)=U(g;h,k).
\]
The two-edge support has stabilizer generated by
$(A\,B)(C\,D)$ and $(A\,C)(B\,D)$; their identities are
$V(-g,-h)=V(g,h)$ and $V(h,g)=V(g,h)$. The star and all-group
rows have constant values $d$ and $1$. Group charge constraints
are preserved throughout. This proves proper transport for all rows.

For reflection, reverse the group arrows and use $(C\,D)$.
This preserves the marked faces of~\eqref{eq:algebraic-tetra-tensor}
and gives the exact coefficient comparison
\begin{equation}\label{eq:algebraic-tetra-reflection}
 T_\tau(u,v;w,z)=\frac{T(-u,-v;z,w)}{a(u)a(v)}.
\end{equation}
Both sides have support $w=u+z$; their ratio there reduces to
$a(u)^2\chi(u,u)=1$. At $A,B$ the factors are precisely the
conversions $v_u'=a(u)^{-1}v_{-u}$ and
$v_v'=a(v)^{-1}v_{-v}$, while the top and interior labels become
$v_z'$ and $v_w$. For the one-edge and two-edge rows, the same
arrow reversal and permutation give
\[
 U_\tau(g;h,k)=U(-g;k,h),\qquad
 V_\tau(g,h)=V(-g,h).
\]
The all-group parameters change by $(g,h,k)\mapsto(-h,-g,k)$;
for the star use $(A\,B)$ instead, giving
$(g,h)\mapsto(g+h,-h)$. Their constant values remain $1,d$.
Reflection replaces each mixed vertex by its prescribed opposite.
The inverse theta factors already present in dual-basis contractions
are preserved, since $\tau(d)=d$; reflection introduces no additional factor.
Finally, $QR_\tau=R^{-1}Q$ and $Q^{\mathsf T}BQ=B_\tau$
extend these comparisons to every marked corner and its dual
contraction.

head: environment

label: prop:channel-singular-values
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:channel-singular-values}
Work over $\mathbb C$. Let $G$ be finite abelian of order $n$, let
$d=(n+\sqrt{n^2+4n})/2$, and assume only
that $\chi$ is nondegenerate symmetric, $a(-g)=a(g)$,
$a(g+h)\chi(g,h)=a(g)a(h)$, $\beta(0)=-d^{-1}$, and
$\beta(g)\beta(-g)=a(g)/n$ for $g\ne0$.
For the channel matrix $T$ in \eqref{eq:algebraic-channel-blocks}, set
\[
 D=\operatorname{diag}(d^2I_n,d^{-1}I_{n^2}),\qquad
 U=D^{1/2}TD^{-1/2}.
\]
Here $T^\dagger$ denotes the conjugate transpose. Then
\[
 T^\dagger DT=\operatorname{diag}(d^2I_n,d^{-1}\Lambda),\qquad
 \Lambda_{(p,q),(p,q)}=
 \begin{cases}1,&p+q=0,\\ n|\beta(p+q)|^2,&p+q\ne0.\end{cases}
\]
In particular, $U$ has singular values $1$ with multiplicity $2n$,
and $\sqrt n|\beta(g)|$ with multiplicity $n$ for every $g\ne0$
(counting coincident singular values with their multiplicities).
They occur in reciprocal pairs. The matrix $U$ is unitary if and
only if the scalar reflection equation holds.
head: environment
name: Exact channel singular values

title: Proof
body_md:
All values of $a$ and $\chi$ have modulus one. Direct multiplication
of the four blocks of $T$ gives the entries of $\Gamma=T^\dagger DT$:
\begin{align*}
 \Gamma_{W_g,W_h}&=d^2\delta_{g,h},\\
 \Gamma_{W_g,H_{pq}}
 &=n a(g)(d^{-1}+\beta(0))\delta_{p,-g}\delta_{q,g}=0,\\
 \Gamma_{H_{pq},H_{rs}}
 &=\delta_{p,r}\delta_{q,s}
 \left(\frac{n}{d}|\beta(p+q)|^2
                 +\frac{n}{d^2}\delta_{p+q,0}\right).
\end{align*}

For the last identity, the matrix-unit supports first force $p=r$,
and the character sum then forces $q=s$. The group components have
the same support. When $p+q=0$, the parenthesis is
$n/d^3+n/d^2=1/d$, using $d^2=n(d+1)$. Thus the displayed Gram
matrix follows without any reflection hypothesis. Its eigenvalues,
after the diagonal normalization by $D$, are the squared singular
values asserted. The product equation gives
$(\sqrt n|\beta(g)|)(\sqrt n|\beta(-g)|)=1$.
For $g\ne0$, the reflection equation is equivalent to
$|\beta(g)|^2=1/n$ by the same product equation; at zero it follows
from $\beta(0)\in\mathbb R$.

label: thm:algebraic-reconstruction
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:algebraic-reconstruction}
  Let $ G $ be a finite abelian group of order $ n $.
Let $K$ be a field in which $n=|G|$ is invertible, and let
$(d_\varrho,\chi,a,c,\beta)$ be a $K$-valued solution of the TPE system for $G$. Then the scalar data reconstruct a spherical fusion category
over $K$ with fusion rules $G+n$.
head: environment
name: Algebraic reconstruction

title: Proof
body_md: Under the strict monoidal and pivotal conventions and the trivial Frobenius--Schur indicator assumption of Section (3), the tetrahedral table constructed from a TPE solution satisfies the pentagon equations by \cite[Theorem~1.1 and Theorem~5.3]{LPR}; hence the standard fusion-category reconstruction gives the required spherical near-group fusion category.
head: environment

label: thm: reconstruction
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{thm: reconstruction}
Work over $K=\mathbb C$. {Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of order $n$}, $d_\varrho=(n+\sqrt{n^2+4n})/2$. let
$(d_\varrho,\chi,a,c,\beta)$ be a solution of the unitary TPE system for $G$. Then the scalar data reconstruct a unitary fusion
category with fusion rules $ G+n $.
head: environment
name: Unitary reconstruction

label: eq:reconstruction-unitarity
title: Proof
body_md:
The values of $\chi$ and $a$ have modulus $1$, and the Gauss
normalization gives $|c|=n^{-1/2}$. Together with
\eqref{eq:beta-reality}, these identities identify the algebraic
involution $\tau$ with ordinary complex conjugation on the
tetrahedral data.
Proposition~\ref{prop:channel-singular-values} now gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reconstruction-unitarity}
 T^\dagger D_{\rm ch}T=D_{\rm ch},\qquad
 D_{\rm ch}=\operatorname{diag}(d_\varrho^2I_n,d_\varrho^{-1}I_{n^2}).
\end{equation}
Since $D_{\rm ch}$ is positive,
rescaling the channel bases by their positive theta norms makes $T$
unitary. A theta norm here is the Hermitian closure $B(v,Jv)$ after
bending, not the bilinear self-pairing $B(v,v)$. These norms are products of trivalent fusion-basis norms,
times the common outer trace factor $d_\varrho$: a rooted vertex with
output $X$ has squared norm equal to its theta value divided by $d_X$.
Thus the normalization is induced by one choice of orthonormal fusion
bases. In these bases the other changes are the unitary corner matrix
$R$, permutation matrices and phases. The resulting fusion
associators are therefore unitary, giving a unitary fusion category.
head: environment

label: cor:unitarity-defect
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:unitarity-defect}
Under the assumptions of Proposition~\ref{prop:channel-singular-values}, put
\[
 \mathfrak d(\beta)=\sum_{g\in G}|\beta(g)|^2-(1-d^{-1}).
\]
Then
\[
 \mathfrak d(\beta)=\frac12\sum_{g\in G}
 (|\beta(g)|-|\beta(-g)|)^2\ge0,
 \qquad
 \|U\|_{\mathrm F}^2-(n+n^2)=n^2\mathfrak d(\beta).
\]
The following are equivalent: scalar reflection, $\mathfrak d(\beta)=0$,
and unitarity of $U$. Reflection is automatic at every $g\in G[2]$.
Consequently every positive-root scalar solution on an elementary
abelian $2$-group reconstructs a unitary fusion category.
head: environment
name: A single nonnegative unitarity defect

title: Proof
body_md:
Expand the squares using
$|\beta(g)||\beta(-g)|=1/n$ for $g\ne0$ and
$(n-1)/n+d^{-2}=1-d^{-1}$. Summing the squared singular values in
Proposition~\ref{prop:channel-singular-values} gives the norm formula.
At an involution $g\ne0$, the product identity gives
$|\beta(g)|^2=1/n$ directly. Unitary reconstruction then follows from
Corollary~\ref{thm: reconstruction}.
head: environment

label: thm:unitarity-gap
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:unitarity-gap}
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of order $n$, and let
$(d,\chi,a,c,\beta)$ satisfy the TPE system over
$\mathbb C$, with $d=(n+\sqrt{n^2+4n})/2$. Put
\[
 p_g=n|\beta(g)|^2,\qquad t=p_0=\frac1{d+1},\qquad
 q_g=\sum_{k\in G}p_kp_{g-k}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:positive-convolution}
 p_gp_{-g}=1,\qquad q_g=p_gq_{-g}\qquad(g\ne0).
\end{equation}
Let $\kappa>1$ be the unique root in $(1,\infty)$ of
$X^3-2X^2-X+1=0$, so $\kappa=2.24697960\ldots$.
Either the tuple satisfies Hermitian reflection, or
\begin{equation}\label{eq:unitarity-gap}
 \max_{g\ne0}\sqrt n\,|\beta(g)|>\sqrt\kappa.
\end{equation}
In particular, the coarse inequalities
$\sqrt n\,|\beta(g)|\le\sqrt2$ for all $g\ne0$
already imply Hermitian reflection and unitary reconstruction.
More precisely, every nonunitary tuple must have $n\ge5$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:unitarity-gap-finite-n}
 M^{2/(n-2)}<(M-1)(1-M^{-2}),\qquad
 M=\max_{g\ne0}p_g.
\end{equation}
In particular, every positive-root algebraic scalar tuple with
$n\le4$ satisfies Hermitian reflection.
head: environment
name: A uniform gap from the unitary locus

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\chi$ and $a$ take values of modulus $1$, Equation~\eqref{eq:betapm}
gives
$p_gp_{-g}=1$ for $g\ne0$, and $\beta(0)=-1/d$ gives
$t=n/d^2=1/(d+1)\in(0,1)$.
For fixed $g\ne0$, taking absolute squares of the cubic TPE and summing
over $h$, character orthogonality gives
$$
\frac1n\sum_{k\in G}
|\beta(g-k)|^2|\beta(k)|^2
=
|\beta(g)|^2
\sum_{h\in G}
|\beta(-h)|^2|\beta(h-g)|^2.
$$
Multiplying by $n^3$ yields the second identity
in~\eqref{eq:positive-convolution}.

If every nonzero $p_g$ is one, the quadratic equation gives
$\overline{\beta(g)}=\beta(-g)/a(g)$, so Hermitian reflection holds. Otherwise set $M=\max_{g\ne0}p_g>1$ and choose
$g$ with $p_g=M$. Then $g\ne-g$, hence $n\ge3$.
Put $\delta=M-1$, $e_0=0$, and $e_k=p_k-1$ for $k\ne0$.
Every nonzero $p_k$ lies in $[M^{-1},M]$, and
\[
 |e_k|\le\delta,\qquad e_{-k}=-e_k/p_k.
\]
Expanding $p=\mathbf1+(t-1)\delta_0+e$ gives, for $g\ne0$,
\[
 q_g=n-2+2t+2\sum_k e_k+2(t-1)e_g+(e*e)_g.
\]
Since $q_g=Mq_{-g}$ and $e_g-e_{-g}=\delta(1+M^{-1})$,
\begin{align*}
 (e*e)_g-(e*e)_{-g}
 &=\delta q_{-g}+2(1-t)\delta(1+M^{-1})\\
 &>\delta(n-2)M^{2/(n-2)}.
\end{align*}
To obtain the last inequality, retain the $n-2$ terms of $q_{-g}$
with $k\ne0,-g$. Their product is $M^2$: indeed,
$\prod_{k\ne0}p_k=1$ and removing $p_{-g}=M^{-1}$ leaves
product $M$, in each of the two factors. The arithmetic--geometric
mean inequality now gives $q_{-g}>(n-2)M^{2/(n-2)}$.
On the other hand, reindexing the second convolution gives
\[
 (e*e)_g-(e*e)_{-g}
 =\sum_{k\ne0,g}e_ke_{g-k}
       \left(1-\frac1{p_kp_{g-k}}\right).
\]
For $x,y\in[M^{-1},M]$ one has
\[
 |(x-1)(y-1)(1-(xy)^{-1})|
 \le\delta^2(1-M^{-2}).
\]
Indeed, its left side equals
\[
 \left|\frac{x-1}{\sqrt x}\right|
 \left|\frac{y-1}{\sqrt y}\right|
 \left|\frac{xy-1}{\sqrt{xy}}\right|,
\]
whose first two factors are at most $\delta/\sqrt M$ and whose
third factor is at most $M-M^{-1}$. Consequently the convolution
difference is at most $(n-2)\delta^2(1-M^{-2})$. Combining this
with its strict lower bound proves~\eqref{eq:unitarity-gap-finite-n}.
Its left side is greater than one, so
\[
 1<(M-1)(1-M^{-2}),\qquad M^3-2M^2-M+1>0.
\]
The function $(M-1)(1-M^{-2})$ is strictly increasing for $M>1$,
which gives $M>\kappa$. Since $\kappa>2$, the simpler sufficient
bound follows. For $n=3,4$, the left side
of~\eqref{eq:unitarity-gap-finite-n} is at least $M$, whereas the
right side is less than $M$, a contradiction. For $n=1,2$ all
nonzero elements are involutions and already have $p_g=1$.
head: environment

label: cor:coarse-defect-bound
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: A coarse scalar bound for unitarity

title: Proof
body_md:
If reflection fails, choose $g$ realizing $M>\kappa>2$ in
Theorem~\ref{thm:unitarity-gap}. Since $g\ne-g$, its reciprocal pair
contributes $(M+M^{-1}-2)/n$ to the nonnegative defect of
Corollary~\ref{cor:unitarity-defect}. Monotonicity of $x+x^{-1}-2$
for $x>1$ gives both strict bounds; that corollary's norm identity
gives the last formulation.
head: environment

label: prop:rm-normalization
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:rm-normalization}
Let
\[
 A_n=\begin{pmatrix}n+2&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \mathbf r_{n,k}=\binom{k/n}{k/n},\qquad
 \mu_n=e^{\pi i(n-1)/12}.
\]
For every $0\leq k<n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rm-value}
 E_n(k)=F_{A_n}^+\bigl((0,-k)\bigr).
\end{equation}
For $1\leq k<n$ this value also equals
$\mu_n\operatorname{shin}_{A_n}^{\mathbf r_{n,k}}
(\varepsilon_n)^{-1}$.
head: environment
name: Real-multiplication normalization

title: Proof
body_md:
At zero both sides of \eqref{eq:rm-value} are
$\sqrt{\varepsilon_n}$, by Proposition~\ref{prop:F-identities} and
\cite[equation~(2)]{RadchenkoWheeler}. For $1\leq k<n$, the matrix
$A_n$ fixes $\varepsilon_n$ and satisfies
$(A_n-I)\mathbf r_{n,k}=(k,0)^{\mathsf t}$, so
$A_n\in\Gamma_{\mathbf r_{n,k}}$.
Scaling the gamma periods and using the standard double-sine/Faddeev
conversion \cite[\S2.3]{RadchenkoWheeler} gives, with
$z_{n,k}=k(\varepsilon_n-1)/n$,
\[
 F(k)=S_2(1+z_{n,k};\varepsilon_n,1)
 =\Phi_{S,0,0}(z_{n,k};\varepsilon_n)
   e^{P_{\varepsilon_n}(1+z_{n,k})},
\]
where
\[
 P_\varepsilon(Z)=\frac{\pi i}{2\varepsilon}
 \left(Z^2-(\varepsilon+1)Z+
       \frac{1+3\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2}{6}\right).
\]
Since $(\varepsilon_n-1)^2=n\varepsilon_n$,
\[
 P_{\varepsilon_n}(1+z_{n,k})
 =\pi i\left(\frac{n-1}{12}-\frac{k(n-k)}{2n}\right),
\]
and therefore $s(k)F(k)=\mu_n\Phi_{S,0,0}
(z_{n,k};\varepsilon_n)$.

Write $T=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$
and $S=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
Then $A_n=T^{n+2}S$, and the eta transformation laws give
\[
 \mu_{A_n}=e^{\pi i(n+2)/12}e^{-\pi i/4}=\mu_n.
\]
On the upper half-plane the defining products
\cite[equation~(1)]{RadchenkoWheeler} give
$\Phi_{A_n,0,0}(z;\tau)=\Phi_{S,0,0}(z;\tau)$:
both have denominator parameter $e^{-2\pi i/\tau}$ and argument
$z/\tau$. Meromorphic continuation gives the same identity at
$\tau=\varepsilon_n$. For $\mathbf u=(0,-k)$ the fixed-point
argument is
\[
 \frac{u_1\varepsilon_n+u_2}{\varepsilon_n^{-1}-1}
 =z_{n,k},
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:rm-value}. Finally the reciprocal conversion to
$\operatorname{shin}$ has correction factor $1$, because the second
coordinate of $(I-A_n)\mathbf r_{n,k}$ is zero
\cite[Definition~4.18 and Proposition~4.19]{Kopp}.
head: environment

label: prop:finite-coefficient-field
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:finite-coefficient-field}
The field
\[
 L_n=\mathbb Q\bigl(\zeta_{4n},E_n(k):k\in C_n\bigr)
\]
is a number field, stable under ordinary complex conjugation. It
contains all scalar coefficients of the TPE system
and $K_n=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{\Delta_n})$.
Exactly $[L_n:K_n]$ embeddings $\iota:L_n\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$
send $d_-$ to $d_+$.
head: environment
name: A finite coefficient field

title: Proof
body_md:
\cite[Theorem~1]{RadchenkoWheeler} give algebraicity of $E_n(k)$;
at zero this also follows from $E_n(0)^2=\varepsilon_n$.
Moreover
\[
 \sqrt{\Delta_n}=2E_n(0)^2-(n+2)\in L_n.
\]
The phases $s(k)$ lie in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_{4n})$, as does
$\sqrt n$ by
\begin{align*}
  \sum_{g\in C_n}^{} a(g) = \sqrt{n}e^{\pi i(n-1)/4}.
\end{align*} 
Its phase is a power of
$i$ for odd $n$, and $\zeta_8\in\mathbb Q(\zeta_{4n})$ for even $n$.
Hence $\beta(k)=E_n(k)/\sqrt n$, $a(k)$, $\chi(g,h)$, $d_-$,
and $c=\beta(0)/\sum_k\beta(k)$ all belong to $L_n$.
Positivity of $F(k)$ and $s(k)^2=a(k)$ give
$\overline{E_n(k)}=a(k)^{-1}E_n(k)$, proving conjugation stability.
Finally each embedding of $K_n$ has $[L_n:K_n]$ extensions to $L_n$,
because number fields are separable.
head: environment

label: cor:all-cyclic-neargroup
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:all-cyclic-neargroup}
For every $n\geq1$, the fusion ring $C_n+n$ has a spherical
categorification with noninvertible simple dimension $d_-$.
Every embedding $\iota:L_n\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$ with
$\iota(d_-)=d_+$ transports it to a pseudo-unitary spherical
categorification.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:algebraic-reconstruction} over $L_n$ and then
extend scalars along the chosen embedding. At the positive root the
simple dimensions are $1,d_+$, so the global dimension equals the
Frobenius--Perron dimension
\cite[Definition~9.4.4]{EGNO15}.
head: environment

label: prop:unitary-galois-criterion
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Unitary Galois criterion and sufficient bounds

title: Proof
body_md:
The scalar identities survive under $\iota$. The transported values
of $\chi,a$ are roots of unity, and character orthogonality and the
Gauss equation give $|\iota(c)|=n^{-1/2}$. Thus the algebraic
reflection agrees with ordinary complex conjugation on those
parameters. The remaining condition is
\eqref{eq:unitary-galois-criterion}.
For $1\leq k<n$, set $S_k=\iota(s(k))$, $X_k=\iota(F(k))$
and $r=\iota(\sqrt n)\in\{\sqrt n,-\sqrt n\}$.
Since $s(n-k)=s(k)$, $F(n-k)=F(k)^{-1}$ and $a(k)=s(k)^2$,
the two sides of \eqref{eq:unitary-galois-criterion} are
\[
 r^{-1}S_k^{-1}\overline{X_k}
 \quad\text{and}\quad r^{-1}S_k^{-1}X_k^{-1}.
\]
They agree exactly when $|X_k|=1$. At zero the equation is automatic,
because $\iota(\beta(0))=-d_+^{-1}$ is real.
The first sufficient bound follows from
Theorem~\ref{thm:unitarity-gap}, since
$\sqrt n\,|\iota(\beta(k))|=|\iota(F(k))|$ for $k\ne0$.
For the second, $d_+^{-2}=n^{-1}-d_+^{-1}$ turns the bound into
\eqref{eq:coarse-defect-bound}; apply
Corollary~\ref{cor:coarse-defect-bound}.
Finally use Corollary~\ref{thm: reconstruction}.
head: environment

label: conj:unitary-galois
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj:unitary-galois}
For every $n\geq2$ and every embedding
$\iota:L_n\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$ with
$\iota(\sqrt{\Delta_n})=-\sqrt{\Delta_n}$,
\[
 |\iota(E_n(k))|=1\qquad(1\leq k<n).
\]
head: environment
name: Cyclic unitary Galois conjecture

label: prop:small-rank-unitarity
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $n\leq4$, Theorem~\ref{thm:unitarity-gap} applies to every
positive-root scalar solution.

For $n=5$, Proposition~\ref{prop:rm-normalization} identifies our
solution with the cycle-$(7)$ example of
\cite[\S4.3]{RadchenkoWheeler}. Its nonzero values are products of
roots of unity and roots of
\[
 P(Z)=Z^4-Z^3-\frac{3+3\sqrt5}{2}Z^2-Z+1.
\]
After any embedding reversing $\sqrt5$, divide the conjugate
polynomial by $Z^2$ and put $W=Z+Z^{-1}$. This gives
\[
 W^2-W-\frac{7-3\sqrt5}{2}=0,
 \qquad W=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{15-6\sqrt5}}2.
\]
Both traces lie in $(-2,2)$, so all roots have modulus one.

For $n=6$, put
\[
 r=F(0)=\sqrt{4+\sqrt{15}},\qquad
 X=F(1)+F(5),\qquad Y=F(2)+F(4).
\]
Reciprocity gives $F(5)=F(1)^{-1}$, $F(4)=F(2)^{-1}$ and
$F(3)=1$. Proposition~\ref{prop:cubic-reduction} gives directly
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^5s(k)F(k)=\sqrt6\,r\,e^{5\pi i/12}
 =r+e^{5\pi i/12}X+e^{2\pi i/3}Y+e^{3\pi i/4}.
\]
Equating real and imaginary parts after multiplication by
$e^{-5\pi i/12}$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:n6-exact-traces}
 X=\frac{2+\sqrt{15}+\sqrt3}{2},\qquad
 Y=\frac{(\sqrt3+1)r-\sqrt6}{2},
\end{equation}
using $\sqrt6\,r=3+\sqrt{15}$ in the original embedding.
If $\iota(\sqrt{15})=-\sqrt{15}$, then
\[
 \iota(X)=\frac{2-\sqrt{15}\pm\sqrt3}{2}\in(-2,2).
\]
Also $\iota(r)^2=4-\sqrt{15}>0$, so $\iota(r)$ is real and
every possible choice of the remaining signs satisfies
\[
 |\iota(Y)|\leq
 \frac{(\sqrt3+1)\sqrt{4-\sqrt{15}}+\sqrt6}{2}<2.
\]
Indeed $\sqrt{15}>15/4$, $\sqrt3<7/4$ and $\sqrt6<5/2$
bound the last expression by $31/16<2$.
The conjugate traces of both reciprocal pairs lie in $(-2,2)$,
and hence all four conjugated values lie on the unit circle;
the midpoint remains $\iota(F(3))=1$.
head: environment

label: rem:arithmetic-content
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:arithmetic-content}
\label{rem:galois}
The algebraic scalar equations survive under every field embedding;
ordinary complex conjugation need not. On $\iota(L_n)$ the
transported involution is
$\iota\circ\overline{(\,\cdot\,)}\circ\iota^{-1}$, which can
differ from ordinary conjugation. Likewise the gamma integral
evaluates the original real embedding, not $\iota(F(k))$:
formally conjugating its periods is analytic continuation, during
which the separating contour crosses poles, rather than Galois
transport. The scalar product identity gives only
$\iota(\beta(g))\iota(\beta(-g))=\iota(a(g))/n$ for $g\ne0$;
reflection requires $|\iota(\beta(g))|^2=1/n$.
This is the real/unitary distinction described in
\cite[\S6]{RadchenkoWheeler}.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:hilbert-twelfth}
For $K_n=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{n(n+4)})$, Proposition~\ref{prop:rm-normalization}
identifies $E_n(k)$ for $1\leq k<n$, up to roots of unity and
inversion, with real-multiplication values of the Shintani--Faddeev
modular cocycle. Kopp's limit formula \cite[Theorem~1.1]{Kopp}
relates squares of these values, with explicit root-of-unity factors,
to exponentials of derivatives at $s=0$ of differences of ray class
partial zeta functions. The Stark conjectures predict their
class-field placement and Galois behavior, as explained after
Conjecture~\ref{conj:unitary-galois}; algebraicity alone is already
unconditional by Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-coefficient-field}.
This is the connection with Hilbert's twelfth problem: constructing
abelian extensions through explicit analytic special values
\cite{Stark1976,AFK}. The categorical application uses the predicted
Galois behavior to obtain unitarity; it does not assert that this cyclic
family generates all abelian extensions of $K_n$.
